Needs an immediate life-saving intervention: airway or breathing support, emergency medication, or hemodynamic intervention (e.g. pulseless, apneic, unresponsive).
High-risk situation, new confusion, lethargy or disorientation, or severe pain or distress: should not wait.
Danger-zone vital signs in an adult (HR over 100, RR over 20, or SpO2 under 92%): consider up-triaging to Level 2.
Stable, but expected to need two or more resources (e.g. labs plus imaging, IV fluids).
Stable, expected to need one resource.
Stable, expected to need no resources beyond examination.
Resuscitation: arrest or imminent arrest needing immediate intervention (e.g. cardiac or respiratory arrest, unresponsiveness, severe shock, severe respiratory distress).
Emergent: potential threat to life, limb or function needing rapid intervention (e.g. altered mental status, moderate respiratory distress, hemodynamic compromise, severe pain).
Urgent: could progress to a serious problem needing emergency intervention (e.g. mild respiratory distress, moderate pain).
Less urgent: related to age, distress or potential to deteriorate; benefits from treatment within 1-2 hours.
Non-urgent: acute but non-urgent, or part of a chronic problem; can be delayed or referred.
Assess and treat in order: airway, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure; fix each problem before moving on and reassess after any change.
High-quality CPR: compressions 100-120/min, at least 5 cm (2 in) deep in adults, full recoil, interruptions under 10 seconds; check pulse for no more than 10 seconds.
Without an advanced airway: 30 compressions to 2 breaths.
Shockable rhythm (VF or pulseless VT): defibrillate as soon as possible, then resume CPR immediately.
Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes during cardiac arrest.
IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg of 1 mg/mL (max 0.5 mg in adults) into the anterolateral thigh; repeat after 5-15 minutes if needed.
Epinephrine is first-line; antihistamines and corticosteroids do not replace it and must not delay it.
Lie the patient flat with legs raised (sitting up if breathing is difficult); avoid sudden standing or sitting.
Recognise stroke with BE-FAST and establish the last-known-well time.
Check blood glucose and get brain imaging to exclude hemorrhage before IV thrombolysis, which eligible patients can receive within 4.5 hours of last known well.
Direct pressure first; for life-threatening limb bleeding pressure can't control, a tourniquet 5-8 cm (2-3 in) above the wound, not over a joint, with the time recorded.
Primary survey: control catastrophic external bleeding, then airway with cervical-spine protection, breathing, circulation, disability, exposure.
Encourage coughing while it's effective; if the cough becomes ineffective, back blows and/or abdominal thrusts until the object clears.
Infants under 1 year: 5 back blows then 5 chest thrusts; never abdominal thrusts.
If the person becomes unresponsive, start CPR; look in the mouth before breaths and remove only a visible object.
Protect from injury, don't restrain or put anything in the mouth, time the seizure, recovery position once it stops; check blood glucose.
A seizure lasting 5 minutes or more is status epilepticus: first-line benzodiazepine (IM midazolam, IV lorazepam or IV diazepam).
Hypoglycemia (under 70 mg/dL / 3.9 mmol/L): if able to swallow, 15-20 g fast-acting glucose and recheck in 15 minutes; if not, glucagon or IV dextrose.
DKA: IV fluids first, then insulin; check potassium before insulin and hold insulin if K is under 3.3 mmol/L.
Repeated inhaled short-acting beta2-agonist (e.g. salbutamol); controlled oxygen to SpO2 93-95% in adults.
Systemic corticosteroids early; add ipratropium for severe attacks; consider IV magnesium sulfate if not responding.
Drowsiness, confusion or a silent chest are life-threatening signs: escalate to critical care urgently.
Within the first hour: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics, give broad-spectrum antibiotics.
For hypotension or lactate of 4 mmol/L or more, 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid early; vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line) to a MAP of 65 mmHg or more.
Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes (worthwhile up to 3 hours after injury); no ice; remove jewellery and clothing that isn't stuck.
Estimate %TBSA (rule of nines; the patient's palm is about 1%); large burns need formula-guided IV fluids, 2-4 mL x kg x %TBSA over 24 hours with half in the first 8, titrated to urine output.
Signs of inhalation injury (facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot, hoarseness, stridor): assess the airway early and consider early intubation.
